analysis.one_liner: Lets workers sue workplace discrimination as a group, restoring a path the Supreme Court closed.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 64 House Democrats, never received a hearing or a vote and died in the House Judiciary Committee at the end of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2011 the Supreme Court, in Wal-Mart v. Dukes, made it much harder for workers who faced the same kind of discrimination to sue together as one group. This bill would create a new legal route for workers to bring those group cases under federal anti-discrimination laws — including laws against discrimination based on sex, race, disability, and genetics — using an easier standard than the Court required. It died without any committee action or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who face discrimination in pay, promotion, firing, or hiring at large companies. Discrimination claims are usually small-dollar cases, so many victims can afford to sue only by joining together; the bill reopens that door after the Supreme Court largely closed it in Wal-Mart v. Dukes.

how_it_helps.text: Lets one or more workers sue on behalf of a whole group affected by the same employment practice, if they show by a reasonable inference that the group is large, the claims are typical, and a significant portion of the group was harmed [S2].

Specifically allows group challenges to 'subjective employment practices' — workplaces where supervisors make pay and promotion decisions by unguided personal discretion — and says that supervisors applying discretion differently does not block the group case [S2].

Restores what the bill's findings describe as the pre-Wal-Mart rule, under which a group case could proceed if the class was united by a common issue of law or fact, a test courts historically applied permissively [S3].
Lets workers choose this new group-action route or a traditional class action, whichever is easier to certify [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large employers, especially big retail and service companies, face much greater exposure to group discrimination lawsuits, including litigation costs and potential back-pay awards. Those costs could also be passed to consumers or affect hiring, though the bill leaves existing limits on remedies intact.

drawbacks.text: The 'subjective employment practice' definition covers any company where managers use personal judgment in personnel decisions — which describes most workplaces — so critics would argue it invites large, costly group suits over ordinary discretion rather than clear discrimination [S2].

The certification standard requires only a 'reasonable inference' that a practice harmed a significant portion of the group, a much lower bar than the Supreme Court's requirement of convincing proof of a companywide discriminatory policy, raising the risk of coercive settlements in weak cases [S2].

The bill lets courts deny individual remedies only if the employer proves the worker would not have gotten the job or benefit anyway, which shifts the burden to employers and could produce remedies for group members with thin individual claims [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill restores a meaningful way to enforce rights that Congress wrote into law but that became hard to use after Wal-Mart v. Dukes, since individual discrimination claims are often too small to litigate alone. The cost falls mainly on large employers in the form of broader litigation exposure, and the lower certification bar does raise a real risk of sprawling suits over managerial discretion. On balance it is a worker-favorable bill whose design questions are legitimate but secondary to its core effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Constitution subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on June 20, 2012, joined by 38 original cosponsors, and 64 House Democrats cosponsored it in total [S1].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on June 20, 2012, and on June 28, 2012 to the Subcommittee on the Constitution; the record shows no further action [S5].
The bill responded to the Supreme Court's 2011 Wal-Mart v. Dukes decision, which required convincing proof of a companywide discriminatory policy before workers could sue as a class [S2].
No committee or subcommittee hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large employers avoided the broader group-lawsuit exposure the bill would have created; workers gained nothing because it never advanced.

industries.industry: Large employers (retail, service, and other big workforces)
industries.note: The bill would let thousands of employees sue together over pay, promotion, and hiring discrimination, sharply raising litigation exposure for companies with big workforces and manager-discretion systems — the very targets of Wal-Mart v. Dukes. Workers' enforcement gain comes directly at these companies' expense [S2].

industries.industry: Employment defense law firms and employer-side HR consultants
industries.note: Group cases would create more demand for workers' counsel and less billable work defending piecemeal individual claims, shifting where discrimination litigation is fought and won [S3].
A reopened group-action route makes many otherwise unaffordable discrimination claims viable, expanding the market for attorneys representing workers [S3].
